title: Delineating Oxidation Aspects of an Additively Manufactured Nanoprecipitation-Strengthened Al<sub>0.2</sub>Co<sub>1.5</sub>CrFeNi<sub>1.5</sub>Ti<sub>0.3</sub> High-Entropy Alloy.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: An additively manufactured (likely laser powder bed fused) Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy produced in an as-built state and possibly with a post-build heat treatment. The base microstructure is an FCC matrix strengthened by nanoscale L12-type (Ni,Co)3(Al,Ti) precipitates (gamma'-like) formed via Al/Ti additions to a CoCrFeNi-rich matrix.
recollection.intervention: Guess: Isothermal and cyclic oxidation testing in air or dry oxygen between about 700 and 1000 C (with thermogravimetric mass-gain measurements), coupled with post-exposure characterization by XRD, SEM/EDS, and TEM (possibly APT) to identify oxide phases, internal oxidation, and precipitate stability. Comparison of as-built versus homogenized/aged conditions to delineate the role of AM microstructure and nanoprecipitates on oxidation.
recollection.structure: Guess: A duplex oxide scale forms with an outer (Ni,Co)(Cr,Fe)2O4 spinel (and some NiO/CoO) and an inner Cr2O3-rich layer; localized TiO2 nodules appear on the surface and an internal oxidation zone develops with fine Al- and Ti-rich oxides beneath the scale. Near-surface regions exhibit depletion/dissolution of L12 nanoprecipitates and oxidation penetrations along melt-pool or grain boundaries typical of AM microstructures.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: Oxidation is controlled by selective Cr oxidation to Cr2O3 and outward cation diffusion through the spinel, giving parabolic kinetics; the low Al content is insufficient for a continuous Al2O3 scale, so Al and Ti undergo internal oxidation, with Ti favoring TiO2 formation and contributing to subsurface depletion of strengthening precipitates. Additive manufacturing-induced microsegregation and high defect density (cellular substructure, melt-pool boundaries, pores) provide fast diffusion paths that localize and accelerate oxidation; heat treatment that homogenizes chemistry and reduces defect density improves scale continuity and reduces mass gain.
recollection.results: Guess: Parabolic rate constants on the order of 10^-6 to 10^-5 mg^2 cm^-4 s^-1 at 800–900 C with an apparent activation energy around 150–180 kJ/mol; after ~100 h at 800–900 C, total oxide thickness ~1–3 μm and a continuous Cr2O3 inner layer. As-built material shows roughly 20–40% higher mass gain (and faster kp) than heat-treated material due to microsegregation/defects; cyclic oxidation below 900 C shows limited spallation, increasing at higher temperatures. Near-surface L12 precipitates are depleted/dissolved by Al/Ti oxidation, with a measured hardness decrease of about 5–10% in the oxidized layer relative to the bulk.

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies comparison of as-built and heat-treated/aged states under oxidation, but misses the specific 750°C/50 h aging treatment and introduces unsupported cyclic testing. Its duplex/trilayer scale description is substantially correct, including spinel/mixed outer oxides, protective Cr2O3, and internal Al/Ti-rich oxidation. The selective-Cr mechanism and inability to form continuous Al/Ti oxides are broadly right, but it incorrectly claims heat treatment reduces mass gain; the aged alloy actually gained more mass. The estimated activation energy of 150–180 kJ/mol is close to the measured ~153–154 kJ/mol, but other numerical claims are unsupported and the stated mass-gain ordering is reversed.
